title: Ang 855–857: Kabir in Bilaval
tomorrow: can you talk to God that bluntly? one Bhagat did.

cards: Someone posts a video of themselves dancing badly at a wedding, and the comments split: "cringe" or "icon." On ang 855, Kabir writes his own version.
In paraphrase: I haven't studied the books, I don't know how to argue; hearing and singing God's praise, I've gone mad. And here's the strange part. He sounds delighted about it.

teach.b: Kabir's hymns in Bilaval open with the world as a show where nobody gets to stay. Then the madness.

teach.h: I'M MAD; THE WORLD IS SANE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: O father, I'm mad; the whole world is sane, and I'm mad. I'm ruined; let no one else be ruined like me. So, the puzzle.
Why would a poet brag about being crazy, then warn everyone not to follow him? One way to read it: listen to who's using the words.
"Sane" is the world's word for people who keep their place, their arguments, their careful image. "Mad" is what the world calls Kabir, because he's stopped playing that game.
He says where the madness came from: hearing and singing God's praise.
So the brag is a joke turned on the people judging him, and the warning is the punchline. Don't get ruined like me, he says, in a hymn that practically invites you to.
Then, on ang 856, he pokes the important people again.
In paraphrase: no king is equal to the Lord; the kings of this world last four days, an old way of saying a little while, and put on a false show.
Here's what's worth telling a friend tonight: the Granth keeps a hymn where a weaver calls himself a madman, and means it as praise.
Kabir's joy is the freedom of someone who no longer needs the crowd to call him sane.

how: Kabir's hymns are sung in kirtan in their ragas alongside the Gurus' own; in Bilaval his playful 'mai bauraa' hymn sits on ang 855.

games.q: Kabir in Bilaval — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir calls himself mad as an insult to himself
it's a joke turned on those who judge him; his madness is praise.
Kabir says the kings of this world last four days
four days: an old way of saying a little while. no king equals the Lord.
in this hymn Kabir says the books and arguments make you wise
he says he hasn't studied them, and went mad singing God's praise.

games.q: a classmate turns down a prestige internship to volunteer at a shelter, and people call her crazy. what would Kabir's hymn on ang 855 notice?
o: 'mad' can be what the world calls someone who stopped playing for status.
if everyone calls it crazy, it probably is; Kabir agrees.
every unusual choice is holy; Kabir blesses all of them.
games.why: Kabir's 'madness' is what the 'sane' world calls a life turned toward God. the hymn doesn't bless every odd choice, but it does question the crowd's word.

practice: Before the sit, send one person a short message about something you're glad about today: no explaining, no polish. Then rest for the sit with that small, unguarded gladness. If you'd like, read Kabir's hymn on ang 856 first.
